unit.title: Models with numbers: variables, constraints, objective

lesson.title: Whole numbers and yes-or-no choices
lesson.subtitle: Why you can’t hire a fraction of a bus, and what rounding gets wrong

video.title: Whole numbers and yes-or-no choices
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Mr Joseph Mwangi — computer studies teacher, Kenya (main character)
Ms Amina Bello — primary teacher, Nigeria (cameo)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer)

scenes.visual: Amina with a clipboard beside a school gate; a minibus and a bus with seat counts and prices; ‘2.13 buses?’ on the clipboard.
scenes.animation: The two vehicles drive in; the number 2.13 wobbles.
scenes.narration: Sixty-four of us are going on the trip. A minibus seats fourteen for three hundred coins, a bus thirty for five hundred and fifty. The maths says two point one three buses. What do I do with point one three of a bus?

scenes.visual: Title card with the Darsi mark and the Optimization track chip.
scenes.animation: Mark pops in; title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: whole numbers and yes-or-no choices, and why rounding isn’t enough.

scenes.visual: Three cards: a bus (1, 2, 3…), a box with yes/no, a cup of rice (any amount).
scenes.animation: Cards flip in; the fraction on the bus card is crossed out.
scenes.narration: Some decisions come only in whole numbers: buses, beds, teachers, desks. Others are yes or no: take this load, or leave it. A linear program allows fractions, which makes it fast. But you can’t hire part of a bus.

scenes.visual: Two buses with four people left on the pavement; then three buses with empty seats and a big price tag.
scenes.animation: The four people wave; the price tag drops on the three buses.
scenes.narration: So round it? Round down to two buses, and four people stay behind: the plan breaks a limit. Round up to three buses, and it costs one thousand six hundred and fifty coins.

scenes.visual: Amina at the gate with two buses; three answer cards drop in.
scenes.animation: Cards bounce in one by one.
scenes.narration: Quick check! The maths said two point one three buses, and I booked two. What went wrong?

scenes.visual: Two buses and a minibus, every seat filled; a price tag 1,400 beside the crossed-out 1,650.
scenes.animation: The minibus drives in; the old price is struck through.
scenes.narration: Four people had no seat. Search the whole-number plans instead: two buses and a minibus seat seventy-four, for one thousand four hundred coins. That’s the cheapest plan that seats everyone.

scenes.visual: A dot grid inside the garden shape: only the dots are allowed; a yes/no switch beside it.
scenes.animation: Dots appear across the shape; a switch flips 0, 1.
scenes.narration: A model whose variables must be whole numbers is an integer program. When they can only be zero or one, they are yes-or-no variables. Integer programs are much harder, because the best plan is no longer at a corner.

scenes.visual: Six load tiles, each with a 0/1 switch; a weight bar fills as switches turn to 1.
scenes.animation: Switches flip; the bar fills; the points counter rises.
scenes.on_screen_text: The truck, as yes or no
scenes.narration: Back to the truck for the village school: six loads, one thousand kilos. Each load gets a yes-or-no variable: one means take it, zero means leave it. The weights taken must add up to at most a thousand. The goal: the most points.

scenes.visual: A code card types out the four lines; the answer appears under it.
scenes.animation: Lines type in; the answer slides up.
scenes.narration: In Python, with Google’s OR-Tools, that model is a few lines. One yes-or-no variable per load, one limit on the weight, one goal. The solver answers: desks and books, sixty-five points, a thousand kilos exactly.

scenes.visual: Two trucks side by side: greedy with solar panels (60) and the best with desks and books (65); a small table fills underneath.
scenes.animation: The greedy truck loads first; the table fills cell by cell.
scenes.narration: A quick rule, most points per kilo first, scores only sixty. Integer solvers search more cleverly. Dynamic programming fills a table of smaller trucks, and branch and bound skips plans that can’t win.

scenes.visual: The left-behind loads on the school yard; villagers and teachers around a points chart, a pencil changing a number.
scenes.animation: The loads fade; a hand rewrites a points value.
scenes.narration: But look at what stays behind: the solar panels, the water filter, the footballs. The points are a judgement: who set them, and did the village school have a say? If the filter keeps pupils healthy, maybe it must go.

scenes.visual: A phone with the lab: the truck, the two methods compared, and the table with outlined cells.
scenes.animation: A finger taps the buttons; the outlined cells light up one by one.
scenes.narration: In the app, pack the truck greedily, then show the best load. Open the table underneath and follow the outlined cells back from the corner: each step takes a load or skips it.

scenes.visual: Mr Joseph holds the water filter tile; three answer cards appear.
scenes.narration: Your turn. The village school says the water filter must go on the truck. In the model, what changes?

scenes.visual: The answer card gets the check; four summary lines and a takeaway bar.
scenes.animation: Lines tick in; the takeaway slides up.
scenes.narration: A new limit: take-filter equals one. Remember: whole numbers and yes-or-no choices need an integer program. Rounding can break a limit or cost more. And people decide what the points mean.

scenes.visual: Amina’s class with paper buses and minibuses on desks, seat counts and prices on the board.
scenes.animation: Paper buses move into rows; totals appear on the board.
scenes.narration: Try it in class tomorrow: plan the trip buses with your pupils. Give them the people, the seats and the prices. Groups find the cheapest whole-number plan that seats everyone, then compare it with rounding the fraction.

checkpoints.prompt: The maths said 2.13 buses, and Amina booked 2. What went wrong?

options.text: Two buses cost more than three

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — 2 buses seat 60, so 4 of the 64 stay behind. Rounding down broke the limit.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — 2 buses seat only 60 of the 64 people. Rounding down broke the limit.

checkpoints.prompt: The water filter must go on the truck. What changes in the model?

options.text: The goal: the filter’s points count double
Nothing: the solver will take it anyway

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — a rule that must hold is a constraint: take-filter = 1. The solver finds the best load around it.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — the best load leaves the filter behind, so the solver won’t take it unless a constraint says take-filter = 1.
